summary: Defines a way to check that an MPLS label switched path really works in the data plane. A probe called an MPLS echo request travels along the path and an echo reply reports the result, helping find failures that normal ping may miss.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8029 defines a way to test whether an MPLS path forwards traffic correctly. The test follows the path's labels and returns results that can reveal where a failure occurs.

questions: what udp port does mpls ping use
what is an mpls echo request
subtitle: A diagnostic probe checks an MPLS path using the same labels as ordinary traffic.

tldr.problem: An MPLS path can drop or misroute user traffic without the control plane detecting the failure, and operators need to locate the fault.
tldr.mechanism: An MPLS echo request follows a label-switched path and carries information about the forwarding class being tested. Routers return echo replies with results for end-to-end checks or hop-by-hop tracing.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8029 consolidates and obsoletes RFC 4379, RFC 6424, RFC 6829, and RFC 7537. It is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 8611, RFC 9041, and RFC 9570.

today: RFC 8029 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 4379, RFC 6424, RFC 6829, and RFC 7537. It updates RFC 1122 and has been updated by RFC 8611, RFC 9041, and RFC 9570.

sections.title: What LSP Ping Checks
sections.content:
An MPLS Label Switched Path (LSP) can fail to carry user traffic even when the control plane does not detect a problem. RFC 8029 defines MPLS echo requests and replies to detect data-plane failures and help locate them.

In ping mode, a request checks whether it reaches an egress router for the tested forwarding equivalence class (FEC). In traceroute mode, transit routers respond hop by hop and provide information that helps compare actual forwarding with the control plane's view.

The request follows the same label-based data path as traffic in the FEC. The RFC focuses on checking the data plane; it does not define a control-plane-only test.
sections.plainLanguage: The test checks whether packets for a particular path reach the right routers. A ping checks the end of the path, while traceroute asks routers along the way to report what they see.

sections.title: Keeping Diagnostic Packets on the Test Path
sections.content:
The request is forwarded by its MPLS label stack, not by its IP destination address. It uses an address from 127/8 for IPv4, or the corresponding range in an IPv4-mapped IPv6 address. The RFC relies on hosts discarding these addresses and routers not forwarding them, reducing the chance that a misdirected diagnostic packet reaches a user.

The sender chooses an address and UDP source port that can help exercise different equal-cost paths. The request uses UDP destination port 3503, IP TTL 1, and a Router Alert option so routers can inspect the OAM message.

Periodic ping can check connectivity. Traceroute can reveal a fault, but the RFC cautions that frequent traceroutes place a greater burden on transit routers.
sections.plainLanguage: The request is routed by its MPLS labels and uses a special destination range that ordinary hosts discard. A Router Alert helps routers inspect the test packet.

sections.title: The Echo Message
sections.content:
An MPLS echo request or reply is a possibly labeled IPv4 or IPv6 UDP packet. Its payload starts with version and flag fields, then identifies whether the message is a request or reply and how a reply should be sent.

The fixed fields also include a return code and subcode, a sender's handle, a sequence number, and send and receive timestamps. The handle and sequence number help match replies to requests. The remaining payload can contain Type-Length-Value (TLV) items.

Reply modes include no reply, a UDP reply, a UDP reply with Router Alert, or a reply through an application-level control channel. A no-reply request can support one-way connectivity checks.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message identifies its type, the requested reply method, and values that help match it to a test. Optional data after these fields describes the path or reports details.

sections.title: FEC Stacks, TLVs, and Results
sections.content:
Every echo request must include a Target FEC Stack TLV that describes the path being tested. Its entries identify the forwarding classes in label-stack order. A stack can name a single destination or include the tunnel and VPN portions of a route.

TLVs carry additional information such as downstream routers and labels. Their values are padded to a four-octet boundary. Types below 32768 are mandatory: an implementation that does not understand one must report that fact. Higher types are optional and should be ignored when unsupported.

The echo reply's return code reports a result. Code 3 means the replying router is an egress for the FEC at the indicated depth; code 8 means the label was switched at that depth. Other codes report issues such as a missing label entry or a mapping mismatch.
sections.plainLanguage: The required FEC stack tells a router which path the test is checking. The reply uses a code to say whether the router is the destination, forwarded the label, or found a problem.

sections.title: Sending and Processing Requests
sections.content:
In ping mode, the sender sets the outermost MPLS label's TTL to 255. In traceroute mode, it starts at 1 and increases the TTL by one for each step. The request includes the label stack and FEC information, and traceroute should include a Downstream Detailed Mapping TLV.

A router sends a recognized request to its control plane, checks that it is well formed, and examines the labels and their forwarding operations. A transit router can report label switching and downstream paths. An egress router checks the FEC against its own mapping.

The reply returns to the request's source address and UDP port, with IP TTL 255. For traceroute, the sender can use downstream information from one reply to form the next request. This can test alternate equal-cost paths, though the RFC notes that full coverage may not be possible.
sections.plainLanguage: Traceroute lets each request reach one step farther, so routers can report their part of the path. The sender uses those replies to test later steps and, where possible, alternate paths.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC identifies denial of service from excessive echo traffic, forged or altered requests and replies, and unauthorized discovery of network details as risks.

Implementations are recommended to limit LSP ping traffic sent to the control plane and check request source addresses against an access list. Replies include values that let the sender match them to outstanding requests. Operators can also use filtering at administrative boundaries.

The Pad TLV can carry data that the receiver ignores, so the RFC notes it could be used as a hidden channel. The special destination range applies to LSP ping traffic on UDP port 3503.
sections.plainLanguage: Test packets can consume router resources or reveal network details. Routers should limit requests and check that senders are allowed to run the test.

sections.title: Registries and Earlier Specifications
sections.content:
The RFC assigns UDP port 3503 to LSP echo requests and replies and describes registries for message types, reply modes, return codes, TLVs, and related fields. It also registers the special use of the 127/8 address range for this diagnostic traffic.

RFC 8029 combines changes that had appeared in earlier LSP ping specifications and updates. It obsoletes RFC 4379, RFC 6424, RFC 6829, and RFC 7537, and updates RFC 1122.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC gives LSP ping a registered port and organizes its message codes and fields. It brings the earlier LSP ping documents together in one specification.
